subject: Lycurgus Cup
title: This 1,600-Year-Old Roman Cup Turns Red When You Light It

scenes.text: This Roman cup is green, until you shine a light inside it.
Then the whole thing glows blood red. It was made around the year 300.
For decades, nobody could explain it. In 1990, a microscope cracked the trick.
Specks of gold and silver hide in the glass, each under a thousandth the width of a salt grain.
Specks that small bounce green light back, but let red light through.
The Romans used nanotechnology sixteen hundred years before the word existed. Now light it again.

description:
The Lycurgus Cup, a Roman glass cup from around 290 to 325 AD, looks green in normal light and glows red when lit from inside.
In 1990, researchers found the answer under the microscope: gold and silver nanoparticles about 50 to 70 nanometres across, scattered through the glass.
The cup is in the British Museum, which bought it in 1958.
How do you think the Romans got the recipe right without a microscope?
first_comment: It is one of only about 40 Roman glass cage cups that survive, and glassmakers still struggle to copy its color trick. Would you dare drink from it?
